extracted.intended_audience: pastors, theologians, clergy, and educated readers of Christian doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and distinctions for what counts as worship, idolatry, and legitimate religious uses of images and ceremonies; plus a definition of philosophy and what is excluded from it. Aimed at assessing religious practices and doctrinal claims against scripture and reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Worship
rubrics_metrics.description: Worship (cultus) is the outward words and actions that signify inward honor or fear of offending and desire to please; to pray, to swear by, to obey, to be diligent and officious in serving are all forms of worship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honor is properly internal, but its outward signs (words, gestures, actions) are called worship. Examples given: praying, swearing, obedience, service. Distinguishes sincere versus feigned acts: both are 'worship' insofar as they are signs of honor; the text emphasizes examining inward intention though the outward acts are the usual measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Divine and Civil Worship
rubrics_metrics.description: Civill worship is the honor shown to fellow humans in authority (kings, magistrates); Divine worship is that shown to that which is thought to be God. The same external act may count as civil or divine depending on the object and intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/anti-patterns: falling prostrate before a king who is thought only a man = civil worship; removing one's hat in church is divine worship. Praying to a king for things he can do is civil, but praying to him for things only God can do (e.g., fair weather) is divine worship and thus idolatry. The linguistic distinction (Greek douleia vs latreia) is explained: latreia is general service; douleia more properly the slave's absolute service. Use the object/intention to classify an act.

rubrics_metrics.name: What Counts as an Image
rubrics_metrics.description: An IMAGE in strict sense is a resemblance of some visible thing (phantasms/ideas/idols), produced by impressions on the senses; material images are made in wood, clay or metal, and may represent either real visible objects or phantastic forms of the brain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key limits: there can be no true image of anything invisible or infinite (e.g., God, soul, spirits). Material images can be images of mental fancies (poetic monsters, saints imagined), and an image in the larger sense can be any representation (an earthly sovereign called the image of God). Examples: reflections, dreams, poetic chimaeras, statues made after a fancy. Distinguish between mere representation/monumental uses and religious attributions of presence/power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Idolatry
rubrics_metrics.description: Idolatry is voluntarily performing external acts that signify honoring either the matter of the image (stone, wood, metal) or the phantasm of the brain (the mental image) — or both — and believing the image hears prayers or has divine power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances/anti-patterns: making or worshipping an image without warrant from God or lawful spiritual authority is idolatry (e.g., the Golden Calf). Praying to an image, believing it to be God or to contain God, or attributing divine actions to it (miracles, speech) are idolatrous. Distinguish coerced acts done from fear of punishment (not idolatry in intent) versus voluntary worship (idolatry).

rubrics_metrics.name: When Use of Images Is Not Idolatry
rubrics_metrics.description: Using images or places as means to worship God is not idolatry when they are set up or appointed by God or by lawful religious authority and are used to worship God (not the image), or when images serve as monuments or civil honors rather than objects of divine reverence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the cherubims over the ark and the brazen serpent were set up by God and served as places before which God was worshipped, not objects of worship themselves; prayer turned toward the Temple (when dedicated) is acceptable. Monuments to friends or memorial pictures (civil honor) are permitted. But making images by private authority and dedicating them to religious use (as the Israelites did with the Calf) is unlawful. The test is whether the image/place is appropriated by God's command or by legitimate ecclesiastical/sovereign authority and whether the worship intends God rather than the image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scandalous Worship (Seeming Worship by Example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeming or scandalous worship consists of outward acts of honor (e.g., performing rites to an image) done from fear or for show, which, when done by persons of authority (pastors, teachers), scandalize others and lead them into sin; such scandal is itself a sin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish actors: an unlearned person coerced by a tyrant who privately detests the image commits no scandal if he is not an example to others; but a pastor or eminent teacher who gives external honor without protest (or conceals his detestation) scandalizes brethren and sins. Guidance: if one must obey under threat of death, private detestation is excused but public example matters; pastors must avoid external practices that appear to approve idolatry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited Religious Uses of Painted or Fancy Images
rubrics_metrics.description: Painting or carving images from visions, dreams, or imaginative fancies is not sinful per se, but to hold such pictures as true representations of God, angels, or saints in a way that attributes them real divine power is idolatry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowed uses: pictures as monuments or memorials, or civil honor of the dead. Forbidden use: regarding fanciful images as embodiments that hear prayers or perform miracles. The argument extends to Eucharistic adoration: if the words 'This is my body' are read to mean that consecrated morsels are individually Christ's bodies (implying many bodies), then worship of them as such would be human institution and therefore idolatrous absent scriptural warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonizing Saints and Certain Ceremonies as Relics of Paganism
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices like canonizing saints, processions with images, wax candles, torches, holy water, wakes, carnivals, and other ceremonies are described as relics of Gentile worship retained in the Church and not instituted by Moses or Christ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats such customs skeptically: they were left from pagan conversion, sometimes renamed (Venus to Mary) and later augmented by bishops for worldly reasons. Guidance implied: evaluate ecclesiastical customs for scriptural warrant and beware of pagan origin or worldly ambition as reasons they persist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy Defined and Its Exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy is knowledge acquired by reasoning from the manner of generation of anything to its properties, or from properties to possible ways of generation, so as to be able to produce effects; it does not include prudence (experience), supernatural revelation, learning taken solely on authors' authority, or false doctrines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit exclusions/anti-patterns: Prudence (experience) is not philosophy because it is memory-based and not attained by reasoning; revelation is not philosophy because it is not acquired by reasoning; learning from authority is faith, not reasoned knowledge; false conclusions properly reasoned from understood words cannot be philosophy. Examples of philosophical practice: geometry, astronomy, and other sciences reasoning to general, immutable truths useful to production and measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary Nature of Extraordinary Spiritual Gifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary gifts (casting out devils, speaking in tongues, miraculous protections) were given to the early Church for a limited time when men trusted wholly in Christ; these gifts ceased or were taken away as people sought earthly authority and riches or relied on their own subtlety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used to explain why modern believers do not commonly perform primitive miracles. The guidance is historical/theological: do not demand the same miraculous signs now as proof of faith; recognize such gifts as temporally contingent on the Church's state of reliance on Christ rather than worldly ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion on Spirits and Possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture attests to angels and spirits, good and evil, but does not support the notion of incorporeal apparitions as identical to spectral dreams or visions; while there may be corporeal (subtle, invisible) spirits, Scripture gives no account of human bodies being truly possessed or inhabited by them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for practice: skepticism toward popular beliefs in possession by incorporeal phantasms; the use of exorcism (conjuration) is a later church practice built on belief in incorporeal spirits and does not have the same footing as primitive cures recorded in the New Testament. Evaluate claims of possession and exorcism against scriptural attestations and historical context.
